compare_blocks.body:
Two relatives can arrive on time with everything they need for an appointment. Preparation and familiarity with the clinic can explain that similarity.

The shared I describes where attention and energy tend to go. The shared S describes what information tends to carry weight. Quietness and punctuality tell you little about either preference.

A single decision can involve both axes. Which criteria matter is a T/F question. Which commitments the family can settle now and which should stay open is a J/P question.

### ISFP and ISTJ: two questions about the same clinic instructions

In a fictional appointment, the care team reviews a medication change, a follow-up and whom to contact with questions. Both relatives receive the same instructions. The example is about communication. The care team sets the medical plan.

One consideration is what the plan means for the patient and what would make it practical for him. Another is whether each part meets the same standard for a clear handover: what was confirmed, what is missing and who can clarify it. Either relative can consider both.

A checklist can expose a missing detail. Asking about concerns can surface a question the patient did not get to ask. Both checks are useful at the same visit.

Prior experience may make either relative comfortable taking notes. When the patient is worried, either can pause to listen. Those choices cannot establish type.

Compare the notes with the care team’s written instructions and invite the patient to explain what he understood. Ask the care team to clarify anything that remains uncertain.

compare_blocks.body:
Quietness in a waiting area tells you little about either type. Either person can speak clearly when they need to.

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The six examples give both relatives the same instructions, time, responsibilities and authority to help. The patient and care team make medical decisions.

Each fictional row compares either decision criteria (T/F) or how the family handles a commitment (J/P). Either type can use either approach.

| Shared situation | One consideration | Another consideration | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The family checks a draft summary of the visit | Which clarification would address the patient’s main concern | Whether all parts of the summary meet the same standard for accuracy and completeness | T/F: the patient’s concerns versus a consistent standard for the summary |
| The family needs someone to accompany the patient to a confirmed follow-up | Keep the same two feasible companions available until work schedules are known | Agree on one available companion now and confirm the arrangement | J/P: keeping alternatives available versus settling a commitment |
| The care team has confirmed the plan and the family can help with pickup | Compare the burden each available arrangement would place on the patient and relatives | Apply the same timing and availability criteria to each feasible arrangement | T/F: the people affected versus consistently applied criteria |
| The family needs to organise a routine update after the visit | Leave two feasible times open until people confirm their availability | Agree on one time and say when it will be reviewed if circumstances change | J/P: retaining options versus agreeing on a plan. The care team’s instructions apply in either case |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two relatives can arrive on time with everything they need for an appointment. Preparation and familiarity with the clinic can explain that similarity.

The shared I describes where attention and energy tend to go. The shared S describes what information tends to carry weight. Quietness and punctuality tell you little about either preference.

A single decision can involve both axes. Which criteria matter is a T/F question. Which commitments the family can settle now and which should stay open is a J/P question.

### ISFP and ISTJ: two questions about the same clinic instructions

In a fictional appointment, the care team reviews a medication change, a follow-up and whom to contact with questions. Both relatives receive the same instructions. The example is about communication. The care team sets the medical plan.

One consideration is what the plan means for the patient and what would make it practical for him. Another is whether each part meets the same standard for a clear handover: what was confirmed, what is missing and who can clarify it. Either relative can consider both.

A checklist can expose a missing detail. Asking about concerns can surface a question the patient did not get to ask. Both checks are useful at the same visit.

Prior experience may make either relative comfortable taking notes. When the patient is worried, either can pause to listen. Those choices cannot establish type.

Compare the notes with the care team’s written instructions and invite the patient to explain what he understood. Ask the care team to clarify anything that remains uncertain.

### ISFP and ISTJ: why Fi and Te occupy different positions

In this page’s convention, ISFP has dominant Fi, auxiliary Se, tertiary Ni and inferior Te. ISTJ has dominant Si, auxiliary Te, tertiary Fi and inferior Ne. Both stacks show Fi and Te in different positions. Their Sensing and Intuition processes differ in orientation.

For an introverted type, the dominant process faces inward and the auxiliary faces outward. ISFP’s P identifies outward Sensing (Se), paired with inward Feeling (Fi). ISTJ’s J identifies outward Thinking (Te), paired with inward Sensing (Si). These are positions in the model, with no fixed order of actions.

The Foundation’s overview lists tertiary Intuition as Ne or Ni for ISFP and tertiary Feeling as Fe or Fi for ISTJ. This page uses Ni and Fi. The dominant and auxiliary descriptions stay the same. See the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
The two fictional examples concern communication and coordination. The care team sets medication and follow-up instructions. Both relatives follow the same plan.

When several relatives help, agree who will capture the instructions and who can ask for clarification. Otherwise, everyone may assume someone else took notes.

### ISFP and ISTJ: the clinic visit, getting all three instructions and checking them

(Fictional example) At the same appointment, both relatives hear the same clinician. One useful task is recording the confirmed instructions. Another is inviting their father to say what he understood and what remains unclear. Either type can do both.

Share the tasks according to who is available and familiar with the clinic. With their father’s agreement, one relative could take notes while the other keeps track of questions he wants to ask. Both can refer medical questions to the care team.

Compare what the patient and accompanying relatives understood with the written instructions. If any detail is missing or accounts differ, confirm it with the care team before passing it on. The check helps the family share accurate information.

### ISFP and ISTJ: the family group asking what the doctor actually said

(Fictional example) A cousin asks for an update in the family chat. Their father agrees to share the confirmed follow-up details and one concern he would like help raising. Either type could include both points in the update.

The confirmed details help the family coordinate practical support. The concern gives them a question they can help him take back to the care team.

Agree on which details the family needs, who will help and who will clarify any open questions. Keep private details out of the chat unless the patient wants them shared. Message length and timing cannot identify type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Quietness in a waiting area tells you little about either type. Either person can speak clearly when they need to.

Punctuality, accurate records and remembering appointments depend on habits, experience and support. Either type can develop those skills, and either can miss something.

Nursing, accounting and care work each develop skills that people of any type can learn. A job title cannot establish a type.

J/P describes the model’s outward-facing process. An ISFP can organise a week of transport, and an ISTJ can revise a schedule when circumstances change.

Who takes notes and when can depend on responsibilities, experience and what others have already recorded. A person can do both tasks at different visits.

comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
ISFP and ISTJ share Introversion (I) and Sensing (S). ISFP prefers Feeling (F) and Perceiving (P), while ISTJ prefers Thinking (T) and Judging (J). T/F concerns decision criteria. J/P concerns the approach to the outside world.

- **Introversion (I):** attention and energy tend to turn inward, toward ideas and reflection.
- **Sensing (S):** observable details and concrete experience carry more weight when taking in information.
- **Thinking versus Feeling (T/F):** Thinking gives more weight to logical consistency and criteria that apply across cases. Feeling gives more weight to values and the effect on the people involved.
- **Judging versus Perceiving (J/P):** in type dynamics, ISTJ’s outward auxiliary is extraverted Thinking (Te), a judging process. ISFP’s is extraverted Sensing (Se), a perceiving process. Either type can make a plan or leave a choice open.

Using this page’s convention, ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. ISFP has dominant Fi and inferior Te. ISTJ has auxiliary Te and tertiary Fi. Sources vary in whether they mark the tertiary process as introverted or extraverted.

At the same appointment, either person might record the confirmed instructions or ask what is still unclear. Either can do both. The model cannot predict who takes better care of someone or who acts first.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Two relatives can arrive on time with everything they need for an appointment. Preparation and familiarity with the clinic can explain that similarity.

The shared I describes where attention and energy tend to go. The shared S describes what information tends to carry weight. Quietness and punctuality tell you little about either preference.

A single decision can involve both axes. Which criteria matter is a T/F question. Which commitments the family can settle now and which should stay open is a J/P question.

### ISFP and ISTJ: two questions about the same clinic instructions

In a fictional appointment, the care team reviews a medication change, a follow-up and whom to contact with questions. Both relatives receive the same instructions. The example is about communication. The care team sets the medical plan.

One consideration is what the plan means for the patient and what would make it practical for him. Another is whether each part meets the same standard for a clear handover: what was confirmed, what is missing and who can clarify it. Either relative can consider both.

A checklist can expose a missing detail. Asking about concerns can surface a question the patient did not get to ask. Both checks are useful at the same visit.

Prior experience may make either relative comfortable taking notes. When the patient is worried, either can pause to listen. Those choices cannot establish type.

Compare the notes with the care team’s written instructions and invite the patient to explain what he understood. Ask the care team to clarify anything that remains uncertain.

### ISFP and ISTJ: why Fi and Te occupy different positions

In this page’s convention, ISFP has dominant Fi, auxiliary Se, tertiary Ni and inferior Te. ISTJ has dominant Si, auxiliary Te, tertiary Fi and inferior Ne. Both stacks show Fi and Te in different positions. Their Sensing and Intuition processes differ in orientation.

For an introverted type, the dominant process faces inward and the auxiliary faces outward. ISFP’s P identifies outward Sensing (Se), paired with inward Feeling (Fi). ISTJ’s J identifies outward Thinking (Te), paired with inward Sensing (Si). These are positions in the model, with no fixed order of actions.

The Foundation’s overview lists tertiary Intuition as Ne or Ni for ISFP and tertiary Feeling as Fe or Fi for ISTJ. This page uses Ni and Fi. The dominant and auxiliary descriptions stay the same. See the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

sections.body_md:
The six examples give both relatives the same instructions, time, responsibilities and authority to help. The patient and care team make medical decisions.

Each fictional row compares either decision criteria (T/F) or how the family handles a commitment (J/P). Either type can use either approach.

| Shared situation | One consideration | Another consideration | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The family checks a draft summary of the visit | Which clarification would address the patient’s main concern | Whether all parts of the summary meet the same standard for accuracy and completeness | T/F: the patient’s concerns versus a consistent standard for the summary |
| The family needs someone to accompany the patient to a confirmed follow-up | Keep the same two feasible companions available until work schedules are known | Agree on one available companion now and confirm the arrangement | J/P: keeping alternatives available versus settling a commitment |
| The care team has confirmed the plan and the family can help with pickup | Compare the burden each available arrangement would place on the patient and relatives | Apply the same timing and availability criteria to each feasible arrangement | T/F: the people affected versus consistently applied criteria |
| The family needs to organise a routine update after the visit | Leave two feasible times open until people confirm their availability | Agree on one time and say when it will be reviewed if circumstances change | J/P: retaining options versus agreeing on a plan. The care team’s instructions apply in either case |
| Relatives ask for an update in the group chat | Consider what the patient wants shared and what the recipients need from the update | Apply the same agreed relevance and privacy criteria to every detail | T/F: personal wishes and impacts versus consistent sharing criteria. Both require the patient’s consent |
| The same family plans three months of practical support under the confirmed care plan | Keep several suitable transport and check-in arrangements open | Agree on a regular support schedule and a way to revise it | J/P: keeping logistical options open versus setting a schedule. Neither changes the clinical plan |

Either type can keep accurate records, listen and clarify questions. The useful checks are whether the written summary is complete and whether the patient understands the plan.
sections.title: ISFP and ISTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
The two fictional examples concern communication and coordination. The care team sets medication and follow-up instructions. Both relatives follow the same plan.

When several relatives help, agree who will capture the instructions and who can ask for clarification. Otherwise, everyone may assume someone else took notes.

### ISFP and ISTJ: the clinic visit, getting all three instructions and checking them

(Fictional example) At the same appointment, both relatives hear the same clinician. One useful task is recording the confirmed instructions. Another is inviting their father to say what he understood and what remains unclear. Either type can do both.

Share the tasks according to who is available and familiar with the clinic. With their father’s agreement, one relative could take notes while the other keeps track of questions he wants to ask. Both can refer medical questions to the care team.

Compare what the patient and accompanying relatives understood with the written instructions. If any detail is missing or accounts differ, confirm it with the care team before passing it on. The check helps the family share accurate information.

### ISFP and ISTJ: the family group asking what the doctor actually said

(Fictional example) A cousin asks for an update in the family chat. Their father agrees to share the confirmed follow-up details and one concern he would like help raising. Either type could include both points in the update.

The confirmed details help the family coordinate practical support. The concern gives them a question they can help him take back to the care team.

Agree on which details the family needs, who will help and who will clarify any open questions. Keep private details out of the chat unless the patient wants them shared. Message length and timing cannot identify type.
sections.title: ISFP and ISTJ in two fictional scenarios

sections.body_md:
Quietness in a waiting area tells you little about either type. Either person can speak clearly when they need to.

Punctuality, accurate records and remembering appointments depend on habits, experience and support. Either type can develop those skills, and either can miss something.

Nursing, accounting and care work each develop skills that people of any type can learn. A job title cannot establish a type.

J/P describes the model’s outward-facing process. An ISFP can organise a week of transport, and an ISTJ can revise a schedule when circumstances change.

Who takes notes and when can depend on responsibilities, experience and what others have already recorded. A person can do both tasks at different visits.
sections.title: ISFP and ISTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
If two results differ, check the questionnaire, version, language and scoring notes. Think about whether you answered for a role with strict requirements or a situation where you had more freedom.

Review several decisions where you had similar discretion. Record the options, why you chose one and what constraints mattered. Consider decision criteria (T/F) and settled versus open commitments (J/P) separately. Use the notes for reflection without scoring them.

If the tool provides scores and explains the cutoffs, check each dimension separately. A score close to a cutoff can make the label sensitive to small changes in answers. If the results are hard to compare, leave the conclusion open.
sections.title: ISFP and ISTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
They differ on the third letter, Thinking versus Feeling (T/F), and the fourth, Judging versus Perceiving (J/P).

T/F concerns decision criteria. J/P concerns the outward-facing process, illustrated here by settling a practical commitment or leaving options open. Either type can take notes and ask how a decision affects the patient.
items.question: Which letters differ between ISFP and ISTJ?

items.answer:
In type dynamics, the ISFP’s P points to outward-facing Sensing (Se), leaving Fi as the inward-facing dominant. The ISTJ’s J points to outward-facing Thinking (Te), with Si as the inward-facing dominant.

In this page’s convention, ISFP has dominant Fi and inferior Te. ISTJ has auxiliary Te and tertiary Fi. The tertiary orientation varies by source. These positions cannot establish the quality of anyone’s judgment. See the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp) and [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).
items.question: Why do Fi and Te appear in different positions?

items.answer:
Yes. Either person can follow a procedure or adjust a plan.

Work requirements, training and the situation can explain either behaviour. Reflect on decisions where you had a choice instead of drawing a conclusion from one action.
items.question: Can an ISFP follow strict rules and an ISTJ be flexible?

items.answer:
Ask the patient what help they want. Assign tasks according to who is available and familiar with them.

One person can record the confirmed instructions and another can help ask the patient’s questions. Check for any missing information before leaving. Refer decisions about medication and follow-up to the care team.
items.question: How can two relatives share the work at a clinic visit?

items.answer:
Separate confirmed information from questions that still need answers.

Write down the confirmed follow-up details and any question the patient wants help raising. Choose who will check with the clinic and share the confirmed information with the patient’s consent. Either type can do that.
items.question: When the visit was not handed over clearly, how do they fill the gap?

items.answer:
First check whether the two results are comparable.

Compare the questionnaire, version, language and scoring notes. If the tool reports T/F and J/P separately, check both. A label alone cannot show which answers changed, and there is no rule for which attempt should count.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources**: the definitions of the preferences follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

**Function-stack convention**: this page uses Ni for ISFP’s tertiary Intuition and Fi for ISTJ’s tertiary Feeling. The Foundation’s overview allows either orientation for each. The dominant and auxiliary processes are the same across those alternatives.

**Editorial fiction**: the clinic visit, chat and table are fictional examples of communication. They cannot be used to identify a type.

**Scope**: the examples cover communication and logistics. Follow the care team’s instructions for medical decisions. Assessment results are unsuitable for ranking ability, screening job applicants or predicting relationships. FermatMind uses its own questions and scoring. See the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
